rv.q: What a brilliant piece of must-see Broadway.
Adjmi's astonishing new play, with songs by the former Arcade Fire member Will Butler, delivers far more than a dishy glimpse inside the recording studio during rock's golden age.
Stereophonic is, refreshingly, the real thing.
Those in the audience know the feeling.
I am a longtime Fleetwood Mac fan, and to me the play felt like warmed-over fictionalized history.
But that doesn’t even begin to describe the genius on display at the Golden Theatre.
It’s a lot of play, a lot of life, and when Butler’s luscious, bruised ballads come together and Grover captures it, we levitate beyond time and space.
Stereophonic is a must-experience, rather than simply a must-see.
'Stereophonic' is a unique and singular exploration of the passion and torment that comes with making art that passes the test of time, and I have little doubt that this play will, too.
Stereophonic is a theatrical experience unlike any other, a three-hour journey that immerses you so completely in the world of a 1970s recording studio that you forget you're watching a play.
In terms of fresh ideas about the creative process, the play doesn’t deliver an LP’s worth of insights.
But why we have to be locked in here for over three hours, only Adjmi knows.
I could be impressed by the writing and acting in “Stereophonic” and still be disappointed by it.
This is a wild, thrilling ride.
Stereophonic compels as a poignant character study and needle-sharp comedy.

It runs three hours and 20 minutes, which is arguably much more than the material requires. (The line to the men’s room in the basement lounge area was so long that gents eventually had to be ushered into the ladies’ room; I didn’t get back to my front mezzanine seat until the lights already had dimmed.
